input:
This passage looks at the staffing position in a dispatch office and asks whether it would make sense to take on one additional member of staff in order to reduce the amount of overtime being worked. The office currently employs 15 people on a full-time basis, and over the course of last year overtime accounted for 21% of all paid hours, which is a substantial share by any standard.

At first glance, the arithmetic looks quite attractive. Taking on one more person on a fully loaded basis would cost $89k per year, and in return roughly half of the overtime that is currently worked would no longer be needed. Looked at purely in terms of the annual totals, that can appear to be a straightforward exchange of overtime hours for establishment capacity.

The picture becomes more complicated, however, once the timing of the overtime is taken into account. The overtime is not spread smoothly across the year; instead, it is concentrated in two distinct seasonal peaks, with much quieter periods in between. A new hire, by contrast, is paid for the whole year, in the quiet months just as much as in the busy ones. The $89k is therefore committed in every month, whereas the relief it provides is felt mainly in the peak weeks, when the office is genuinely stretched.

In the end, then, the question is not really whether the office can justify another salary across the year as a whole, but whether covering the peaks with a permanent member of staff is worth the price. Away from the peaks, the extra capacity has little to do, and it is the peak weeks alone that carry the case for the hire.
target:
One additional hire for the dispatch office costs $89k per year fully loaded and replaces half of the overtime the office works. The office employs 15 full-time staff, and overtime ran at 21% of paid hours last year.

Overtime in the dispatch office is not spread evenly across the year. It is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, and between the peaks the present establishment covers the work inside ordinary hours. A staffing change keyed to an annual total therefore misreads the problem the office has. The complication for the staffing case is that a hire is paid for the full year: the salary runs through the quiet months at the same level as through the peak weeks, while the overtime it replaces occurs in the peaks alone.

The hire buys peak cover. In the peak weeks, where the office is short, an additional member of staff in post removes overtime hours that would otherwise be worked, and the removal is worth most where the load is highest. Outside the peaks, the same salary buys capacity the dispatch work does not call on. The trade stands in one sentence: $89k per year, in every month of the year, against relief that arrives in the peak weeks only.

Judged on the year as a whole, the case is weak; judged on the peaks, it is the cost of covering them with establishment staff rather than with overtime. The review makes no claim beyond the peaks: the hire replaces half of the present overtime, and the half it replaces is peak overtime. Whether that cover is worth its price is a judgement on the peak service, not on the annual overtime bill.
